title: Throwing a Ball on the Moon
learningObjectives: Calculate maximum height from vertical speed and gravity using ymax = V0^2 / (2*g).
Explain that horizontal speed stays unchanged while vertical slowing determines the highest point.
Compare the same throw on the Moon and Earth to show lower gravity yields a higher arc.

sources.title: Throwing a ball on the Moon (project-authored test text)
sources.attribution: Written by the Make knowledge interactive project team for testing.

evidence.quote: On the Moon there is no air, so a thrown ball feels no drag at all.

explanations.text: On the Moon there is no air, so a thrown ball feels no drag and its flight is purely ballistic.

evidence.quote: Vertically, gravity slows the ball at a steady rate g.
On the Moon g is about 1.62 m/s^2, roughly one sixth of the 9.8 m/s^2 we feel on Earth.

explanations.text: Gravity slows the rising ball at a steady rate, with Moon gravity about 1.62 m/s^2 compared with 9.8 m/s^2 on Earth.

evidence.quote: The ball stops rising when V = 0, which happens at t = V0 / g.
Because g on the Moon is about six times smaller, the same throw rises about six times higher than on Earth.

explanations.text: The ball stops rising when vertical speed reaches zero, fixing the highest point, so the same throw rises about six times higher on the Moon.

predictions.prompt: A ball is thrown on the Moon with horizontal speed 10 m/s and vertical speed 10 m/s where gravity is 1.62 m/s^2. Predict the maximum height.
A ball is thrown on the Moon with horizontal speed 12 m/s and vertical speed 20 m/s where gravity is 1.62 m/s^2. Predict the maximum height.
The same ball is thrown on Earth with horizontal speed 10 m/s and vertical speed 10 m/s where gravity is 9.8 m/s^2. Predict the maximum height.
